title: Any mention of AI = AI Slop
author: mrjbelfort
selftext:
Apparently if anything uses AI in any way, then it is AI slop. I'd like to think about that narrative a little bit. 

  
Everyone here knows true slop when they see it. Poorly vibe coded sites, littered with bugs, that use that same damn rounded corner react element that they all use with that shitty icon pack. This is sloppy, but it also is a loud minority of the AI space. 

  
Just because a product has AI in it, doesn't mean its instantly "slop", and this narrative gets old quick. A product can intuitively and intelligently integrate AI into its systems, but because its AI, its slop. It dosen't matter how well done it was, how well thought out or carefully integrated, if its AI its slop. 



Integrating AI in a meaningful way where it acts as a tool and not a crutch is the defining factor between actual slop and regular products. 

  
I think the AI slop crowd is going to be really frustrated in another few years when literally everything has AI integrated into it. For gaming espeically, I do not see a world where AI is not heavily used. It makes NPCs come alive, and can allow you to build a game with infinite replayability, and so much more.

  
Oh well, more compute for us I guess

replies.author: mrjbelfort
replies.body:
Yeah the restrictions can get so frustrating, GPT was what I tried first and immediately had to scrap it because of the guardrails. I tried local LLMS but they dont have the processing power needed. 

The new game is going to be centered around NPC interactions. Essentially the player will create a life in a town, and build relationships with the NPCs that inherit it. Each NPC will have their own wants needs and desires, and also work towards things independently of the main character. For instance even if you don't interact with him, your local neighbor might end up running for mayor and winning the votes of the other NPCs, which could have effects on your town. I want to make it open ended like Lifespans and just see where players end up, my main goal is to give players as many options as I can

Things like that become extremely popular and spread like wildfire. These people don't care if they're punching down at broke indie devs - they just want to hurt people. Big corps will be just fine, and they won't touch them at all. Again, it's easiest to just go after people who can't defend themselves, and the easiness of it all is the big attraction to them (whether they know it or not). 

"Slop" means "sloppy", and yes, plenty of AI-generated stuff is sloppy. Used as part of a workflow by competent artists, the outputs aren't sloppy. Indie devs now have a chance. But that doesn't matter right now. 

In 5-10 years, all the preteens making games using Roblox's AI tools will flood the adult market and things will change. But for now, it's largely just mindless anger.

replies.author: cdgalvan
replies.body:
To be fair here.... I'm pretty sure calling Hollow Knight and Team Cherry "Indie" doesn't quite mean the same thing as what a solo dev with no budget is talking about. That is corporate subsidized indie with a decent budget, which is something that people who have certain means to start out with often are able to achieve more so than just somebody with a dream and a full time job that pays crap and takes most of their time and energy.... It's not really a fair comparison. 

And Super Meat Boy is, like... Solidly ok. It's nothing groundbreaking. It was mostly novel because there were so many less people competing in that space at that time. And it was the product of a programmer and an artist collaborating well enough to see something to fruition.... Lots of people try to collaborate with friends and acquaintances, and it's usually not lack of effort that keeps a project from succeeding in many of those cases. Which leads people to attempting to go solo... When you try to collaborate enough times, and it just never works out, you end up coming to the conclusion that you're better off on your own pretty naturally... This is honestly how so many electronic musicians start out as well-- they bounce from one band to another, feeling a constant sense of failure that has little to do with their own effort... Until they decide they are the only person they can reliably count on to make things happen, and they get themselves the required gear and go solo.... 

I don't disagree that AI is not the only way a solo dev can make a game. I also don't think AI automatically equate to low effort in every case. I do think a lot of people lack nuance in these sorts of discussions. 

I think the big thing that AI is promising solo devs is faster iteration time, and the potential to release faster, which might actually allow them to compete in a highly competitive space. I have seen some amazing games that were a solo devs first and last, because they spent so much time on it, years of work... It had amazing art and gameplay.... It was a very high effort product.... and it still failed to make enough income for that dev to survive on. If they had been able to make the same game in a much shorter period of time, the money that was made would be going farther. It might have worked out. 

I'm not saying that there won't be some low effort crap pumped out. That happened before AI, and it will continue to happen. But, it's probably best if we don't make assumptions about folks and what they are making. Instead, constructive feedback, like we are talking about any other game, regardless of how it's made, seems like the best way to help a new generation of devs make better games.

replies.author: Dore_le_Jeune

Joke's on them 😂  
I vibe coded a VR game demo that's basically hide and seek, but using the most realistic math I could for sound propagation and other systems I thought would be fun, like randomly adding a smoker trait to the character on a new game, and that character will light up a cig and the guards you're hiding from can actually smell you and follow you. Certain guards are rolled with smoker stats and those guys wouldn't smell as well, BUT, they may also be rolled with an extra stat that allows them to distinguish if the smell is from a cigarette brand another coworker smokes, and if they two don't match, he may get suspicious. 

I was able to do all this using Claude CLI in maybe a week because of token limits and most of the time spent was honestly finding a usable free model for a proper environment for testing the "game". 

I can only imagine what other creative stuff people can finally try now that anyone with the desire and willingness to take that first step into coding will be able to create.

>"Then you can't afford to make a game." Pissed me off to no end.

Let me offer another perspective. Let's assume you cannot afford to invest money and it's fair, I'm being quoted thousands of Euros for a few models or concept art. Not everybody is willing to risk that.

However, why must AI be the first alternative here?

I don't have the skills to create movie-quality 3d models but I can certainly do some low-poly ones. If I cannot afford 3d models, I would pivot my art direction towards what I can create. With more practice I could certainly improve. Why is this not the first alternative?

replies.author: SirStarshine
replies.body:
Let me explain this way: I was a pretty decent pencil artist as a kid. I've used Photoshop on occasion, not enough to be proficient but I can intuit my way around and do what I need. I've learned the basics of coding but I was never able to get into advanced territory. I've tried to practice 3D modeling but I can't properly create anything that looks that good. And I'm not talking about "I tried 3 months ago and wasn't immediately professional so screw it." I have mental health issues I've been battling for years and continued trying to learn these skills, and never gotten anywhere. It's like an artist's version of "Locked-In" Syndrome, where you have a clear idea, a vision for something you want to do, and even map out all the details, but you just don't have the skills to make it happen. 

I've tried to accomplish something, \*anything\* in game development for the last 14 years, and accomplished exactly squat. Now, with AI, I've been able to begin executing an idea and within a few days, I have satisfactory character animation, environmental objects, a playable level, and soon I'll have a skeleton for a battle system as a proof-of-concept (the only reason I haven't got it now is because of token limitation). And this is not a complex game, but I never would have even made it this far without the use of these new tools that people like to denigrate.

Problem is, it's a text-adventure and just showing a wall of text isn't exactly eye-catching! And I use the images as an immersion tool, so they are part of the game as well, but perhaps going 80% AI artwork isn't the way to go to promote - anyone's thoughts on that would be appreciated?

replies.author: CircularSeasoning
replies.body:
My thoughts: do what you want. No one should be telling you what tools to use to make your vision come alive, else they'd be making the game, not you.

As long as you treat your promotional pieces with the same care and love you put into your game, it should be fine. At a minimum that means no extra fingers and make sure there are no typos in the image. So many lazy people have so far used whatever the first thing is spat out by ChatGPT, etc., and it's obvious "slop" because they make no effort to refine the product. I see this everywhere and I'm like, Yo, this an amazingly detailed and majestic poster but... there are typos in the text within the image! And therefore it looks shit!

Ultimo: All art is artificial. A drawing of a house in the beach sand is not really a house. Get what I am saying?

comments.author: dobkeratops
comments.body:
the term AI is too broad, one must distinguish small nets like animation controllers from the huge generative models trained on internet scrapes.

I see this unresolved, and a lot of issues are being conflated.

if we normalise that AI can be trained on scrapes, then that's a path to the end of any kind of human intellectual or creative work. if this comes hand in hand with cancer cures, robots that look after us, great, but at the minute those things still seem "10+ years away" , whilst the threats to people's livelihood is still there.

I think it's quite feasible based on the progress with gen-AI that we will see complete prompt to game .. whether that's 'autonomous game mods' or world models, or some blend.

a lot of people in the gamedev community are motivated by the craft itself , not the end result, and if that sounds backwards, consider what you're actually adding to the world in training data , if you care about other uses of AI (and AI degrades when trained on it's own output). The type of assets AI produces.. the types of errors .. the process (eg 3d models done by voxelizing producing awkward topology, whereas a human models  gradually capturing salient topology) .

I have mixed views on all of this.. I'm an AI enthusiast running locally, and overall we need AI to help solve the really big problems (fusion energy, getting space resources online, and of course the cliche of curing cancer and other diseases, that's tied in with elderly care) .. and keeping AI out of entertainment marketplaces doesn't hold any of that back. It might even be a forcing function , no quick buck for AI companies on scraping entertainment, they have to go work with people who gather scientific and engineering datasets.

\> and can allow you to build a game with infinite replayability,

see that's pat of the end of games as a business. "ok you've got your infinitely repayable game with infinite variety of newly self-prompted experiences learning what the player wants" .. in that world only one business remains, "datacenter".

comments.author: Paolete_Fulton
comments.body:
I think the problem is people are using “AI slop” as a category when it should be a quality judgment.  

Slop isn’t “contains AI.” Slop is low-effort, derivative, uncurated output with no taste, no iteration, and no real design thinking behind it.  

If AI is doing the thinking for you, yeah, it usually shows. But if AI is just one tool inside a clear creative process, that’s not automatically slop any more than using Unity assets, Photoshop brushes, or procedural generation is.  

The better question is: did the developer make meaningful decisions, or did they just ship the first output? That’s the line people actually care about.

comments.author: Dore_le_Jeune
comments.body:
People hate on AI because they can't get access to their formerly cheap video game cards, plain and simple. They feel that Nvidia owes them something when people with more money (companies) are willing and able to pay more for the cards. Also, gotta remember gamers have been having issues accessing GPUs for a while, with multiple price increases and scalpers just making the whole scene annoying on and off over the years. 

So, instead of being the darling of gamers everywhere (indie games are super popular for a reason, people can get creative if true indie) vibe coders are dismissed with the lowest effort because they assume AI coding is low effort and they're being spoonfed hate by so many different influencers who hopped on to the AI hate bandwagon because it gets views. 

I'll go ahead and happily admit that when I was learning c++ in like 2002ish, BASIC a year earlier, c# and java also over the years (none of them being languages I'm even remotely able to code in anymore as I just dabbled for a few months and moved on with life) I was doing what many others have done in their own journeys that is honestly much worse than probably any generated AI slop within reason: copy and paste code that's \*supposed\* to do what I want, tweak it until it finally works, and move on to the next coding obstacle. If that doesn't go anywhere, ask on Stack Overflow, hope to get answers or find more examples you can tweak, and then maybe try to learn something from tutorials that won't even build as they were written years ago targeting no longer supported/popular tools.
